newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Yamani sells Swiss watchmaker Vacheron to Vendome.
newsitem.headline: Yamani sells Swiss watchmaker Vacheron to Vendome.

text.p: Former Saudi oil minister Sheik Ahmed Zaki Yamani on Thursday sold Vacheron Constantin to Vendome, saying the future of the world's oldest top-quality watchmaker was best assured by a luxury group owner.
Neither Yamani nor Joseph Kanoui, chairman of Vendome Luxury Group, whose brands include Cartier, Piaget and Dunhill, would disclose the price paid after weeks of secret negotiations.
Industry sources estimated Vendome paid between 100 million and 110 million Swiss francs ($77 million to $85 million) for what Yamani called "the jewel of Geneva".
Vendome is 70 per cent owned by South African-controlled Richemont Securities AG and was created three years ago from the rationalisation of Richemont AG, Dunhill Holdings and Rothmans International.
Swiss experts lamented the loss of yet another independent watchmaker, following the acquisitions of Jaeger LeCoultre, Breguet and Baume & Mercier -- the latter by Vendome.
But Yamani, majority shareholder in the Geneva-based Vacheron Constantin since 1987, defended the sale at a news conference where he clearly enjoyed the limelight.
"This is definitely a great day for Vacheron Constantin.

"Today I am happy that all my objectives have been reached with the help of Vacheron management. The number of employees has doubled since 1987 and its shop, offices and factories have all been maintained in Geneva."
Yamani, 66, said he had "donated" Vacherin Constantin to a trust he had set up. The trust would manage the sale's proceeds.
"It is clear to me and to the trust that Vacheron Constantin is better supported in the long-term by having a luxury group owner," he said. "It will be in good hands.
"I am convinced that the Vendome Group will ensure the long-term stability of the Vacheron Constantin brand which is essential to its development."
Created in 1755, Vacheron made 11,091 luxury watches last year, priced from 8,000 Swiss francs up to four million francs.
The private company, which does not release its figures, has posted 25 per cent annual growth since 1987, according to Claude-Daniel Proellochs, managing director who keeps his post.
Roughly 60 per cent of its products are sold in Asia, including Japan, followed by 26 per cent in Europe, 10 per cent in the United States and four per cent in the Middle East.
Vacheron Constantin employs 126 people in Geneva and the Swiss Jura canton (state), as well as 20 people in distribution centres in France, Germany, Italy and the United States.
Kanoui assured the continuity of the Swiss institution: "Vacheron Constantin is Vacheron Constantin and will stay so."
But industry sources expressed disappointment, noting that Patek Philippe, Audemars Piguet, Girard Perregaux and Rolex are virtually the only completely independent luxury watchmakers.
"The big names are disappearing one after another in the pocket of big groups," one industry source said.
With 7,600 employees and 370 boutiques, Vendome Luxury Group had revenues of 2.7 billion Swiss francs and operating profit of 455 million francs in the last financial year.
Yamani, who served 24 years as oil minister for the world's largest oil producer and exporter until he was sacked by King Fahd in 1986, is now an active academic and energy analyst.

Asked his plans, he said: "Vacheron wasn't the main thing in my life. I have the Centre for Global Energy Studies in London, the Islamic Heritage Foundation and I teach law at Harvard University. "I have various activities in Geneva -- cultural, charitable and business as well. My life is extremely full."
